summary_paraphrase: Pabi and her dog Boo set out to find a rainbow with Boo's nose. For each of four colours the nose first finds something that cannot be eaten (socks, soap, a bottle, a ball) and then foods of that colour that can. The finds are gathered, cooked into a colourful meal, and eaten; the last line tells the listener that they can eat a rainbow too.

humor_notes: OBSERVED: the comedy is the wrong find (socks, soap, a bottle, a ball offered as food) answered by a loud No!, and Boo's behaviour in the pictures (head in a bucket, banana on his head). INFERRED: the absurd question is the joke a 3-4 listener can answer out loud.

repetition.description: Sniff, sniff, sniff. on every wrong-find spread
repetition.why: a short sound line the listener can join, set in bold, always in the same slot

repetition.description: wrong find, Can we eat ...? No!, unfinished line; then food word, Can we eat ...? Yes!, adjectives, question to the listener
repetition.why: the yes/no answer is given by the listener before the text gives it; four rounds without variation in shape risk monotony but each round changes colour and joke

repetition.description: Can you think of something <colour> that is good to eat? closes each food spread
repetition.why: hands the turn to the listener at a fixed point; asks for the listener's own answer, not one in the book

repetition.description: the four finds are listed again with their colours
repetition.why: recall before the idea; prepares the rainbow meal

notes: OBSERVED: Boo's rainbow-striped collar carries the motif on every spread; the text never mentions it.
OBSERVED: each wrong find is enlarged on its own on the right-hand page, like a picture-dictionary entry; each food spread shows the two foods large.
OBSERVED: the background colour changes with the colour round.
OBSERVED: a baby (page 6) and an adult cook (page 11, face not shown) appear only in pictures; the text keeps the story to Pabi and Boo.
OBSERVED: Pabi's feelings (disgust at the socks, impatience at the ball) are in her face only.
OBSERVED: the final rainbow has six bands though four colours were found; blue and purple are never hunted.

strengths: a question the listener can shout the answer to on every spread
unfinished line at each wrong-find spread end, completed by a food after the turn
a colour concept carried by a quest instead of a list
title question asked and answered at the end
the listener is invited to name their own food on four spreads
weaknesses: no problem or stakes: the hunt never fails
four identical rounds; the shape never varies
the rainbow is four colours in the text and six in the picture
the adult who cooks is invisible in the text, so the we-cooked claim belongs to an unseen helper
a health message is stated at the end (makes us big and strong)
Boo is referred to with her once and his/its elsewhere only by name

anti_patterns.note: the meal makes us big and strong is told, not shown; mild, and typical of concept books
eight spreads in one fixed two-step shape; the jokes and colours vary but the structure never does. Borderline: for 3-4 the predictability may be the point

child_appeal_heuristic.label: Research heuristic — not validated
child_appeal_heuristic.rationale: Scores are the analyst's reading of the pages, not observations of children.

age_suitability.notes: Gentle concept quest (colours, food) with jokes about inedible things; no peril. Peak research intensity 4 of 5 (anticipation and joy at the meal), about 2 on the engine's 0-3 scale. The Can we eat ...? No! pattern discourages, rather than models, putting objects in the mouth. The jokes about Boo and the adult cook live in the pictures; the yes/no pattern and refrain work in text alone.
